abstract: The author discusses his involvement in Hotpoint's move to a concurrent engineering approach for product engineering. The author focuses on two main aspects, the role of IT on concurrent engineering and supplier relationships. The nature of concurrent engineering though means that they cannot be treated in isolation and many other factors are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Simultaneous or concurrent engineering is often proposed as one approach that encourages the integration of the engineering functions and their supporting systems. Concurrent Engineering is about: efficiency of the design and development process; the ability to develop new products faster; considering the product design as well as the manufacturing and support process; involvement of users in the specification process; and the visibility and control of accurate and timely data. It is a response to competitive pressures to: get products to market in a shorter time; incorporate more features or variety at less cost; and produce more new products, more often by the parallel development of both the product and the associated manufacturing processes and consideration of all elements of the product lifecycle.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Most UK companies are aware of concurrent engineering (CE) and a few have mature implementations generating significant benefits. The vast majority however are confused; they find it difficult to define CE and to decide what benefits they may achieve. Based on work with many companies the author attempts to distil their experiences for the benefit of others. In practice, most companies struggle hardest with the people issues of CE. They also find that, with the benefit of hindsight, the way forward was based on commonsense. The author focuses on the common pitfalls and implementation methods used to create an environment where teamworking and integrated problem solving can work.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

The supply of equipment has traditionally been the last element of a project, which can result in more expensive facilities which are sometimes sub-optimised for production, usually because of inadequate delivery time imposed by previous project slippages. To overcome these problems, concurrent engineering (CE) has become commonplace in the automotive industry, where either major product or face lift programmes are being increased in frequency. Given that production facilities can take between three and 18 months to supply, it has become important to involve suppliers of such equipment as early as possible in the planning cycle. General industry is now using CE, having seen the benefits of lead time reduction and cost savings achieved in the automotive sector because: novel solutions can be fully evaluated through development projects, reducing technical risk and achieving optimum performance; balance of cost vs. performance can be more fully established, i.e. the trade-off between labour effectiveness, automation and risk; eliminating the competitive tender process reduces lead times; and better design through more information being available earlier in the project. An additional benefit for the customer is an element of technology transfer which will mean that customer knowledge gained will significantly enhance future production development processes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Concurrent engineering-why do it at all?
abstract: In striving to maintain their position as a world class supplier of guided weapon systems. British Aerospace Defence Dynamics Division (BAe Def DD) have recognised the need to rapidly implement concurrent engineering (CE) principles and practices. The author, is a member of the Company's Change Team, which is tasked with introducing CE into BAe Def DD, describes why and how the implementation of CE is being addressed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Concurrent engineering project management of supporting systems
abstract: In today's competitive market place there are many pressures on the engineering functions of a manufacturing company. To survive and prosper in such an environment, companies must match the demands of the market place with an effective and efficient means of designing, developing, introducing and manufacturing 'world class products', utilising 'world class processes'. Engineering data management (EDM) has an important role to play in supporting a concurrent engineering approach which expedites and integrates the design, development and manufacturing process. The author focuses on the importance of project managing the introduction of an EDM system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
